content_summary: Published online 19 Nov 2026 (received 13 Jan 2024, accepted 6 Nov 2026) per scanner; DOI 10.1080/15387216.2026.2764063. Not independently confirmed from the publisher page.

Abstract (per scanner): spatial justice is approached through land rent as a key notion; spatial change and land-rent variation are interrelated and mediated by land-rights-based spatial governance; land rent dissipation exacerbates deterioration of spatial quality and leads to social segregation.

Cases (per scanner abstract): (1) Shipai village, Guangzhou, with inadequate spatial governance; (2) an aging, physically deteriorated Shanghai neighbourhood cluster with deficient management; (3) another Shanghai old neighbourhood cluster showing tacit bottom-up collective coordination. Method: empirical investigation plus census data.
Credited mechanism (per abstract): bottom-up collective spatial governance is the defining factor maintaining inclusive communities and achieving spatial justice.

NOT available: how 'land rent dissipation' is defined (Cheung-style dissipation under attenuated property rights vs. loss of rent to non-collective capture vs. rent not reinvested in the commons). The abstract-level text does not settle it; do not assert a Cheung lineage. No figures, sample sizes or page locators obtainable.

content_summary: Essay, 32 pp., written 30 Aug 2026, posted 1 Sep 2026 on SSRN (per scanner).

Thesis (per abstract): while attention was elsewhere the property tax went through a revolution nearly as profound as the 1970s-80s revolt (Proposition 13, Proposition 2 1/2). Many states reformed to give large tax benefits to owner-occupied homes.
Driver: rising property values plus homeowner-dominated politics; because property taxes are wealth taxes, rising wealth produced political anger rather than satisfaction.

Burden shift: services are shifted onto commercial property (including rental apartment buildings), other local taxes and state funding. Reforms turn the property tax from a collective service-provision tool into standard redistributive taxation in which commercial owners pay for homeowner services.
States named in the abstract: Florida, Ohio, North Dakota and Texas 'considered' abandoning property taxation on owner-occupied housing or entirely.

Predicted effects: more state authority over local governments; less stable local funding (but less tax foreclosure in recessions); stricter zoning but more building where legal; higher housing costs, a substantial wealth transfer toward existing homeowners.
No figures in the abstract-level text; no page locators available.

suggested_text:
In a September 2026 SSRN essay, Yale Law School's David Schleicher reads the wave as a second property-tax revolt, comparable to the one behind Proposition 13 and Massachusetts' Proposition 2 1/2. He attributes it to post-COVID rises in property values combined with homeowner-dominated state and local politics: because the property tax is a wealth tax, homeowners whose wealth rose answered with anger rather than satisfaction. On his reading, the reforms shift the cost of local services from owner-occupied homes to commercial property, including rental apartment buildings, other local taxes and state funding, turning the tax from a collective charge for services into a redistributive tax on commercial owners. He predicts greater state authority over local governments, less stable local funding, stricter zoning but more building where it is allowed, and higher housing costs amounting to a wealth transfer to existing homeowners. The essay is unrefereed, and these are the author's interpretations and predictions; only its abstract is publicly available.

Homevoters page, optional sentence: Schleicher's 2026 essay on the property-tax revolt (unrefereed; abstract only) likewise locates the driver in homeowner-dominated politics and predicts higher housing costs as a transfer to existing owners.
